bullets: Marley’s face in the door knocker (Stave 1) foreshadows the ghost’s visit.
Marley says Scrooge has a chance of escaping his fate: hope is foreshadowed.
Scrooge’s ‘surplus population’ (Stave 1) foreshadows the Ghost’s rebuke and Tiny Tim’s danger (Stave 3).
Ignorance and Want foreshadow ‘Doom’ for society.
The phantom in Stave 3’s final line foreshadows Stave 4.
‘Humbug’: Scrooge’s word in Stave 1; he starts to say it after Marley vanishes but stops at the first syllable.
‘Are there no prisons?’ repeated by the Ghost in Stave 3.
‘God bless us every one’: Tiny Tim (Stave 3) and the narrator (Stave 5).
Three Ghosts (Past, Present, Yet to Come), plus Marley.
Tricolons: ‘I will live in the Past, the Present, and the Future’; ‘as good a friend, as good a master, and as good a man’.
Fairy-tale and religious associations (three wishes; the Trinity) make the story feel timeless and complete.

callouts.p: Dickens uses foreshadowing and repetition to make Scrooge’s journey feel inevitable yet open to change, and the rule of three to give the moral fable the satisfying shape of a fairy tale or carol.

exam.q: Explain how Dickens uses repetition to present change. (20 marks)
exam.tip: Pair each repetition: first use → second use → what changed.

mistakes.r: Explain how a repeated line means something different the second time.
mistakes.w: Naming repetition without saying how meaning changes.

quotes.a: The first crack in his certainty.
quotes.q: He tried to say ‘Humbug!’ but stopped at the first syllable
as good a friend, as good a master, and as good a man

summary: Foreshadowing, repetition and the rule of three hold the novella together: early details anticipate later events, repeated words and phrases return transformed, and patterns of three (three Ghosts, tricolons) give the story a fairy-tale, carol-like shape.

terms.d: Hints of what will happen later.
A group of three parallel words or phrases.
